Now I'm not talking about elements of speech like parable and metaphor and simile. I'm not talking about those types of things. I'm talking about the big question, and I have boiled it down to three in my study of Scripture over the last 45 years. God speaks to us in precept, principle, and pattern. A precept is a line item. It is just clear and bold for everyone to see where God says, this is the way, walk in it. These are the thou shalts, thou shalt not, they are mandates, they are words of encouragement, whatever the case is, it's just a line item and it's clear for everyone to see. Now with a precept, sometimes they are interpreted, sometimes they're not, but the fact is they're usually black and white and we either obey or disobey. Rejection of Jesus is going to send you to hell and lack of trust and belief in him. And that's across the board. But the fact is, we have to ask the question, is my behavior, whatever that is, whether it's smoking or drinking or all of those things that we ask about, is it glorifying to God? Is it a stumbling block to others? We will go over those things in the days ahead. But the fact is, there is an underlying principle that we have to follow. Our bodies are the very holy of holies of God himself. So if God lives in us, we need to take care of our bodies and we know that we abuse our bodies when we overeat, when we smoke cigarettes, all of those things. So the greater question is, how can I live in a way that will be pleasing to God? Will honor the body that God's given me, which is important and not overeat and not do things that are damning and dangerous to our bodies like smoking cigarettes and all of those things that we ask questions about. That is the guiding principle. And that is made up of two or more precepts. There is no thou shalt not smoke. And so we have to go back to the principle of the teaching of the Bible says that our bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit, along with many other precepts. And so that would be a principle. And I'll deal with that just a little bit more in a moment. The third is pattern. Many times the Bible doesn't speak to something in precept or in principle, or sometimes just in principle and in pattern, there's no precept on it. In the scriptures, for instance, we observe the life of Jesus, of the prophets, in the New Testament, the apostles, and we see how they did things and we pattern our life after that. The apostle Paul said, mimic me as I mimic Jesus. That's a, he's talking about a pattern of life, a way of life. explicit_propositions.text: God speaks to us in the Scriptures through precept, principle, and pattern.
Precepts are clear, direct commands such as 'thou shalt not' or 'do this'.
There is no biblical command requiring Gentiles to keep Shabbat.
Precepts are typically binary—obeyed or disobeyed—with little room for interpretation.
Paul encouraged believers to imitate his example as he imitated Christ.
Principles are formed by combining two or more precepts into a broader teaching.
The principle behind avoiding harmful behaviors includes honoring God’s presence in the human body as His temple.
Pattern involves observing the lives of Jesus, the prophets, and the apostles to guide Christian living.
Smoking is not explicitly forbidden in Scripture, but its permissibility depends on principles like bodily stewardship.
Observing the Lord's Day (first day of the week) is based on pattern rather than precept or principle alone.

assumptions.text: Scripture contains all necessary guidance for living a godly life.
The Bible is the primary and authoritative source of divine revelation.
The human body is sacred because it houses the Holy Spirit.
Believers should seek to understand God’s will through systematic study of Scripture.
Christian practice should reflect imitation of Christ and early Christian communities.
Interpretation of Scripture requires distinguishing between literal commands and derived teachings.
Spiritual maturity involves moving beyond legalistic thinking toward principled and patterned living.
God communicates primarily through discernible structures within Scripture rather than mystical experiences.
Cultural practices like Sabbath observance require theological reevaluation in light of new covenant theology.
Audiences expect structured, hierarchical frameworks for understanding spiritual truth.
